result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.complement()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Return the complement of the graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L32185-L32269){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.complement() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Complement](/assets/graphs/complement.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A four-node path A, B, C, D. In the complement every pair that was not connected becomes an accent edge (A to C, A to D, B to D), while the three original edges are dropped and shown dashed." width="100%"} Creates a new graph with the same nodes but complementary edges. An edge exists in the complement if and only if it does *not* exist in the original graph. Self-loops are never included. New edges have no attributes and default weight (`1.0` for weighted graphs). For directed graphs, complements directed edges independently in each direction. For undirected graphs, complements undirected edges. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new Graph with complementary edge set. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#53d4d25c .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edge("A", "B") ) comp = graph.complement() comp.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: Every pair that wasn't connected in the original now is, and vice versa: ::: {#2f3d791f .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} comp.has_edge("A", "C"), comp.has_edge("A", "B") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (True, False) ``` ::: ::: This makes it easy to find missing connections in a network -- for example, spotting which pairs of people in a friend graph aren't yet friends: ::: {#af3b9f38 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} friends = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "Diana"]) .add_edges([("Alice", "Bob"), ("Bob", "Charlie")]) ) non_friends = friends.complement() non_friends.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ['Charlie--Diana', 'Alice--Charlie', 'Alice--Diana', 'Bob--Diana'] ``` ::: ::: Comparing a graph to its own complement is one way to check for self-complementary structure: ::: {#7e84ec16 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(directed=False) g.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) g.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("C", "D")]) comp = g.complement() comp.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` ['A--C', 'A--D', 'B--C', 'B--D'] ``` ::: ::: Directed graphs are complemented per-direction, so a missing `A->B` doesn't imply `B->A` was also missing: ::: {#93e898ae .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edge("A", "B") ) comp = g.complement() comp.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` ['B->C', 'B->A', 'C->B', 'C->A', 'A->C'] ``` ::: :::
